h1.u: R E M A R K S

body.p: Careful review and examination of the subject application
are noted and appreciated.
Support for the claim amendments can be found in the

drawings as originally filed, for example in FIGS. 1 and 12, and in the specification as originally filed, for example, on page 11, line 11 through page 12, line 19, page 66, line 22 though page 68, line 26 and page 94, line 14 through page 96, line 8. No new
matter has been added.
The interpretation under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) presented in
the Office Action has been obviated by amendment, in part, and respectfully traversed, in part. In particular, claim 1 and claim 11 have been amended. The capture device element has been deleted.
As such, the interpretation of the capture device element is no longer relevant. Support for the interface element is provided in the drawings, as originally filed, in FIG. 1 and in the

specification, as originally filed, in at least page 11, line 11 through page 12, line 19. In particular, the interface element 104 is described as receiving and/or communicating a number of specific signals. Furthermore, the interface element 104 is described as
implementing one or more specific communication protocols. As such, the claim interpretation for claims 1 and 11 under 35 U.S.C.
§112(f) has been obviated by amendment.
Regarding claim 19, Applicant's representative does not

Representative for the Applicant respectfully disagrees with the interpretation in the Office Action at page 6 that the claimed capture device is at least one of an image sensor, logic or a buffer. The capture device 102a described in the specification and drawings, as originally filed, comprises one or more of the sensor 140a, the logic 142a and the buffer 144a (e.g., and similar descriptions are provided for each capture device 102a-102n with respective sensors 140a-140n, logic 142a-142n and buffers 144a-144n in a scenario where multiple capture devices are implemented). The
sensor 140a, the logic 142a and the buffer 144a are the specific structure of the claimed capture device. A lengthy description of

the specific structure to perform the claimed function is described in the specification, as originally filed, at least on page 17, line 25 through page 19, line 5. The drawings and specification, as originally filed, provide specific structure of the claimed capture device, and describe the details of the structural components of the claimed capture device. As such, the claim
interpretation of claim 19 under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) is traversed.
The rejection of claims 11-12, 14, 16, and 18 under 35
U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over Han (U.S. Patent No.
10,424,204 B1) , in view of Sabeti (U.S. Application No 2015/0175072 Al), and in further view of Nagy (U.S. Application No. 2020/0132803
A1) has been obviated by amendment and should be withdrawn.
The rejection of claim 13 under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being
unpatentable over Han, in view of Sabeti, in further view of Nagy, and in further view of Lavoie (U.S. Application No.2018/0029591 Al)
has been obviated by amendment and should be withdrawn.
The rejection of claim 15 under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being
unpatentable over Han, in view of Sabeti, in further view of Nagy, and in further view of Zhang et al. (U.S. Application 2017/0089720
A1; hereinafter Zhang) has been obviated by amendment and should be
withdrawn.
The rejection of claim 17 under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being
unpatentable over Han, in view of Sabeti, in further view of Nagy, and in further view of Faller (U.S. Application 2021/0133500 Al)
has been obviated by amendment and should be withdrawn.
Han provides collision warnings provided by stationary
vehicles (Title). Sabeti provides vehicle vision system with image processing (Title). Nagy provides radar module for use with
traffic monitoring and predictive analysis systems (Title).
In contrast, claim 11 of the presently claimed invention

provides an apparatus comprising an interface and a processor. The interface may be configured to receive pixel data corresponding to an exterior of a vehicle. The processor may be configured to process the pixel data arranged as video frames, perform computer vision operations on the video frames to detect a moving object in the video frames, determine a predicted path of the moving object, determine a probability of the moving object colliding with the vehicle based on the predicted path, determine a course correction for the moving object to prevent the moving object from colliding with the vehicle, generate a plurality of discrete steps to perform the course correction, and generate a control signal when the probability is greater than a pre-determined threshold. The
control signal may be configured to enable an audio output played

from the vehicle comprising a verbal instruction. The predicted path may be determined by tracking the moving object over time in a sequence of video frames. The verbal instruction may comprise the plurality of discrete steps of the course correction. The plurality of discrete steps comprise instructions for a driver of the moving object. The references, alone or in combination, do not
teach or suggest each of these limitations.
In particular, claim 11 provides determining a course

correction for the moving object to prevent the moving object from colliding with the vehicle. The primary reference, Han, is silent regarding determining a course correction for the moving object to prevent the moving object from colliding with the vehicle, as claimed. At page 8 of the Office Action, col. 4, 11. 9-27 of Han are cited as support for an avoidance action 150. However, Han describes the avoidance action 150 as "an automated movement of vehicle 110 (e.g., by requesting than an automated navigation system move vehicle 110". The vehicle 110 in Han is not the moving object, as claimed. In Han, as shown in FIG. 1, the vehicle 110 is the stationary vehicle and not the moving object 130. As such, Han does not disclose determining a course correction for the moving object to prevent the moving object from colliding with the vehicle, as claimed. At best, Han describes determining a course correction for the stationary object, which corresponds to the vehicle, as claimed, and not the claimed moving object. The

secondary references, Sabeti and Nagy do not cure the deficiencies of Han. As such the combination of references does not teach or suggest determining a course correction for the moving object to prevent the moving object from colliding with the vehicle, as
claimed.
Representative for the Applicant does not agree that the
secondary reference, Nagy discloses determining a course correction for the moving object to prevent the moving object from colliding with the vehicle. At best, Nagy discloses providing a
communication to brake when a vehicle is in a radar detection area.

Even if the communication to brake in Nagy is interpreted as determining the course correction for the moving object to prevent the moving object from colliding with the vehicle, as claimed, claim 11 further provides generating a plurality of discrete steps to perform the course correction. Nagy is silent regarding

generating a plurality of discrete steps to perform the course correction. The communication to brake in Nagy is a single and specific step. Nagy may provide an instruction to brake, and to brake only, but no further information or instructions are provided. In contrast, claim 11 provides a plurality of discrete steps to perform the course correction. The specification, as originally filed, provides specific examples of the discrete steps (e.g., "STOP! Change the gear to forward. Turn the wheel to the right.", etc.) . The primary reference, Han, and the secondary

reference, Sabeti, do not cure the deficiencies of Nagy. Han may disclose human speech auditory warnings, but warnings are not the plurality of discrete steps to perform the course correction, as claimed. In addition, as described above, Han determines the avoidance action 150 for the stationary vehicle and not the moving object 130, as claimed. As such, the combination of references do not teach or suggest generating a plurality of discrete steps to
perform the course correction, as claimed.
Claim 20 is independently patentable over the combination

of references. Claim 20 provides that the plurality of discrete steps comprise an instruction to stop the moving object, an instruction to change a direction of travel of the moving object and an instruction to rotate a steering wheel of the moving object.

The combination of references is silent regarding an instruction to stop the moving object, an instruction to change a direction of travel of the moving object and an instruction to rotate a steering wheel of the moving object, as claimed. At best, Nagy describes providing a brake instruction. No other types of instructions are disclosed. As such, the combination of references does not teach or suggest an instruction to stop the moving object, an instruction to change a direction of travel of the moving object and an instruction to rotate a steering wheel of the moving object, as
claimed in claim 20.
Claim 21 is independently patentable over the combination

of references. Claim 21 provides providing a first of the plurality of discrete steps, determining whether the moving object performed the first of the plurality of discrete steps using the computer vision operations, and providing a second of the plurality of discrete steps in response to determining that the first of the plurality of discrete steps has been performed. The combination of references is silent regarding providing a first of the plurality of discrete steps, determining whether the moving object performed the first of the plurality of discrete steps using the computer vision operations, and providing a second of the plurality of discrete steps in response to determining that the first of the plurality of discrete steps has been performed, as claimed. None of the references disclose checking whether the claimed discrete steps have actually been performed. Without checking whether the discrete steps have been performed, the combination of references cannot determine when to provide a next one of the discrete steps.

As such, the combination of references do not teach or suggest providing a first of the plurality of discrete steps, determining whether the moving object performed the first of the plurality of discrete steps using the computer vision operations, and providing a second of the plurality of discrete steps in response to determining that the first of the plurality of discrete steps has
been performed, as claimed, in claim 21.
The references are silent regarding determining a course

correction for the moving object to prevent the moving object from colliding with the vehicle and generating a plurality of discrete steps to perform the course correction, as claimed. Therefore, the claims include limitations not taught or suggested by the cited
references and the rejection should be withdrawn.
Claims 1-2, 4-10, and 19 have been allowed. The

amendment of claim 1 is not believed to change the scope of the invention with regard to the cited references. Dependent claim 12 has been canceled. Dependent claims 20-22 have been added. Claims 13-22 depend either directly or indirectly from independent claim
11, which is now believed to be allowable.
After a final rejection, an amendment canceling claims

may be made (37 CFR §1.116(b) (1)) and an amendment presenting rejected claims in better form for consideration on appeal may be admitted (37 CFR §1.116(b) (2)). Also, an amendment touching the merits of the application may be admitted upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why the amendment is necessary and was not earlier presented (37 CFR §1.116(b) (3)). The amendments presented herein either cancel claims, present rejected claims in better form for consideration or are necessary to rebut the new ground of rejection presented for the first time in the final Office Action.
The amendments rebutting the new ground of rejection would not reasonably have been presented earlier because the citation to the reference forming the basis for the new ground of rejection was
first present on the record in the final Office Action.
Furthermore, the amendments involve incorporating subject

matter from the cancelled dependent claims and, therefore, are believed to better focus, if not remove issues for appeal, or require only a cursory review by the Examiner in conjunction with the arguments presented to rebut the rejections of the dependent claims. In particular, claim 1 has been entered and allowed and the amendment to claim 1 and 11 is believed to resolve interpretation under 35 U.S.C. §112(f). The amendment to claims 7 and 14 clarify an antecedent issue. The amendment to claim 11 and newly added claims 20-22 narrow the claims to better focus the claims for appeal and/or for the concurrently submitted After Final Consideration Pilot Program request. As such, the amendments presented herein are believed to be compliant with the showing requirement under 37 CFR §1.116(b) (1-3) and Applicant respectfully
requests that the amendments be admitted.
Claims 1, 7, 11, and 14 have been amended. New claims
20-22 have been added. The amendments and new claims do not broaden the scope, which is specifically provided for as proper
under 37 CFR 1.116 when accompanied by a Request for Consideration under the After Final Consideration Pilot (AFCP) program 2.0. Such
a Request is submitted herewith.
Accordingly, the present application is in condition for
allowance. Early and favorable action by the Examiner is
respectfully solicited.
